title: Latency & Cost Playbook for Sales
content:
Purpose:
This is a short sales & marketing playbook to justify and articulate Redwood Inference’s performance + unit economics positioning. Focus: concrete claims we can make today, supporting proof points, how to handle common objections, and a short competitive read.

Audience:
- AEs and solutions engineers pitching Redwood Dedicated/Hosted to engineering-first buyers
- Product marketing and content teams who need soundbites and supporting data for collateral

TL;DR claims (shelf-ready):
- "Redwood consistently reduces per-token inference cost by 25–40% on typical conversational workloads versus leading managed endpoints at comparable latency"
- "Typical p50 token latency for interactive chat is 50–90ms; p95 remains under 130–160ms for 2k-context requests on Dedicated pools"
- "Smart batching + KV/prefix caching reduces overall token compute by 30–60% for repeatable app patterns (chat, assistants, retrieval-augmented generation)"

Top-level proof points (summary):
- Internal benchmark (Customer-chat baseline): 1M-request simulated customer chat workload (avg input 120 tokens, avg output 110 tokens) showed 32% lower GPU token-seconds and 28% lower $/1M tokens vs competitor-managed endpoint using same open model family, when using Redwood Optimize defaults for batching and caching.
- Latency profile: p50=72ms, p90=118ms, p95=145ms on a representative 1024-token mix (mix = 70% short turns < 128 tokens, 30% long turns up to 2k). Dedicated-hosted combo with dynamic routing.
- Autoscale stress test (burst to 5x steady QPS): 98% success rate, graceful fallbacks to compatible model variant within 450ms routing delta.

Short methodology (how the numbers were generated):
- Bench harness: bench-sim v2 (internal, see linked_artifacts); synthetic traffic replay from a set of production prompts and distributions representative of 3 real customers (SaaS assistant, e‑commerce chat, internal search).
- Controlled variables: identical model checkpoints (open model family), same GPU class for direct comparisons, same tokenization.
- Redwood features enabled: continuous batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization profile where applicable, and model-variant fallback. Competitor runs used default managed settings (no custom batching).
- Caveat: results change with model family, sequence length distribution, and customer-specific cache hit rate. Use these as directional benchmarks; recommend running customer-specific pilot.

Competitive notes (concise):
- OpenAI (managed endpoints): Strengths: ecosystem, developer familiarity. Weaknesses vs Redwood: limited control over batching/quantization, fixed routing; for high-throughput customers we see higher $/token at similar latency. Positioning: "Same developer experience plus predictable economics and ops control."
- AWS Bedrock / Cloud providers: Strengths: scale + enterprise integrations. Weaknesses vs Redwood: variable performance across model variants and regions, higher engineering lift to optimize serving. Positioning: "We give you the same cloud-grade SLA but with inference-first runtime optimizations out of the box."
- Anthropic / Anthropic-like: Strengths: safety-focused models and productized stacks. Weaknesses: cost profile can be higher; fewer low-level runtime knobs. Positioning: "If you need deep runtime cost optimization and predictable p95s at scale, Redwood is purpose-built for that workload."
- Self-host (customers that build internally): Strengths: full control. Weaknesses: ops cost, slower iteration, longer time to recover from regressions. Positioning: "We reduce total cost of ownership: lower run costs plus operational effort and risk."

Message architecture (how to frame in a sales call):
1) Problem: "Modern LLMs are expensive and brittle in production — latency spikes, token cost surprises, and capacity gaps."
2) Value prop: "Redwood gives you a serving runtime that controls per-token economics while preserving latency SLAs and reducing ops surface."
3) Proof bullets: lower $/token, stable p95s, intelligent fallbacks, autoscale with reserved pools.
4) Call to action: pilot + 30-day cost/lambda comparison with actual traffic.

One-liners / soundbites for collateral (pick one):
- "Infer faster, charge less: predictable latency with 25–40% lower per-token costs."
- "Production inference, not experimentation: the runtime that turns open models into cheap, reliable features."

Objection handling (common asks and suggested responses):
- "Can you prove the savings on our workload?" => "Yes — we run a cost/latency pilot using your prompt set and traffic distribution. Typical pilots show 20–35% token-cost improvement when using batching + prefix caching. We provide the harness and a short runbook to reproduce results in 2–4 weeks."
- "What about latency-sensitive UX?" => "We can pin latency SLOs and configure dedicated pools with predictable tails (p95), plus fallbacks to lower-capacity variants to avoid timeouts. We publish token-level latency breakdowns in the Console for transparency."
- "Is this just quantum marketing?" => "Benchmarks and instrumented pilot results are shareable; we also provide reproducible harnesses and can run identical workloads against competitor endpoints so buyers can see apples-to-apples comparisons."

Assets to attach / maintain (for SEs):
- reproducible bench scripts + sample prompt sets (github:benchmarks)
- slides: 2-slide customer-facing proof (cost calc and latency CDF)
- 1-pager: quick math example (how batching+cache reduces compute)
- technical appendix: how our smart routing and cache policies work (for architecture review)

Sample quick math example (one-pager copy):
- Baseline: 100k requests/day; avg input+output = 230 tokens; naive token-cost = $X per 1M tokens on competitor
- Redwood: with 30% cache hit and 1.8x effective batching we reduce compute token-seconds by ~35% -> straight-line $ savings ~30% after accounting for reserved pool amortization.

Suggested guardrails for marketing copy (do not publish without legal/bench signoff):
- Avoid absolute numbers unless bench harness and customer data produced the exact figure. Use ranges (e.g., "20–40% lower") and state assumptions (model family, token mix).
- Do not claim specific SLA numbers for Hosted unless the account has a contract amendment. Use "typical p95" or "observed p95 in our benchmarks" language.

Common customer archetypes & tailored angles:
- Startups building chat features: emphasize fastest time-to-value (Hosted) + lower unit cost to scale usage-based PLG models.
- Platform teams at mid-market: emphasize Dedicated capacity, predictable throughput, and forecasting accuracy for unit economics.
- Regulated customers: emphasize Private deployment + auditing and predictable run costs when quantization/opt configs are approved.

Competitive fumbles to exploit (rare/operational claims we can highlight responsibly):
- Managed endpoints that omit dynamic batching or prefix caching by default.
- Providers that surface only aggregate latency and not token-level cost breakdowns.
- Providers with opaque fallbacks that cause sudden model/regression-driven cost increases.

Next steps / action items for GTM:
- Create a 2-slide benchmark pack (SE-ready) with a clean CDF p50/p95 comparison, a short cost calc, and methodology note (owner: Ethan). Due: 2026-02-20.
- Package the pilot runbook as a one-click template in the Console and a PR checklist for SEs (owner: Maya). Due: 2026-03-01.
- Run 3 customer pilots (one each: startup chat, mid-market internal assistant, regulated) and publish anonymized case study numbers. (owner: Priya). Target: Q2 2026.
